passage: I'm Rafiq. I sit next to Jahnavi in Class 10, so I saw her history project feedback sheet when Ma'am handed it back. I counted. Nine ticks, with comments like 'excellent map', 'clear timeline', 'lovely use of sources'. And one line at the bottom in red: 'Conclusion is rushed.' She read it for a long time. At lunch she told Anjali, 'Ma'am hated my conclusion.' After school she told her mother on the phone, 'She said my project was rushed.' Not the conclusion. The project. By evening, in our class chat, she wrote: 'history project was a disaster lol.' I don't know exactly what she felt. But I saw the sheet. It wasn't a disaster. It had nine good things and one thing to fix, and somehow only the red line went home with her.

qa.q: What did the red line on Jahnavi's sheet say?
qa.a: The red line said, 'Conclusion is rushed.'

qa.q: Why might the red line be all Jahnavi remembers?
qa.a: The criticism stung, so Jahnavi's attention kept going back to it, and the hurt made nine good comments fade until one line felt like the whole verdict.

qa.q: What could help Jahnavi see the whole sheet?
qa.a: Jahnavi could read the sheet again and write the nine good comments next to the one fix, then plan how to tighten the conclusion.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see the gap between the sheet and Jahnavi's story about it?
qa.a: Rafiq, who counted the ticks, seems puzzled and a bit concerned that a strong project had become 'a disaster' by evening.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager who got nine praises and one criticism and by evening remembers only the criticism.

passage:
Saturday: At the inter-school science fair, the judge spent ten minutes at Abhinav's solar dryer. 'Clever design. Good data. Very neat poster. Your costing is a little vague, though.' She moved on.
Sunday: Abhinav replayed only one sentence. Costing is vague. Costing is vague. He told Irfan on the phone, 'She basically said the whole thing was vague.' Irfan said, 'Didn't she say clever?' 'Just being polite.'
Wednesday: The score sheet came to school. Irfan read it out in the corridor: design 9, data 9, presentation 8, costing 5. 'That's your one weak spot. Everything else is top.' Abhinav took the sheet and looked at the numbers for a long time. Then he drew a small circle around the 5 and wrote next to it: ask Papa about prices.

qa.q: What score did Abhinav get for costing?
qa.a: Abhinav got 5 for costing.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav dismiss 'clever' as 'just being polite'?
qa.a: The criticism hurt, so it held Abhinav's attention, and the praise felt less believable beside it; the painful line seemed like the judge's real opinion.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Hearing all the scores read out put the 5 next to three high marks, so Abhinav could see one weak spot and plan a fix instead of feeling the whole project had failed.

qa.q: What might Irfan feel reading the score sheet aloud?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt relieved and eager to show the full picture, since the numbers proved what Irfan had been trying to say on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a teenager who hears praise and one criticism from a judge and replays only the criticism until the full score sheet is read out.

passage: Rehana, you've been staring at that one comment on your essay for an hour. Let me tell you about your Jyoti Masi at fifteen. I wrote a story for the school magazine, and the editor, a senior girl, sent it back covered in notes. 'Beautiful opening.' 'This line made me cry.' 'Great dialogue.' I think there were ten good notes. And one: 'The ending feels weak.' Guess which one I remembered? For a month I told everyone the story was weak. I nearly withdrew it. My mother made me sit and read the whole page out loud, every note, slowly. By the end I was embarrassed at how much I'd skipped. I fixed the ending in one evening. The story was printed. So, before you decide your essay is bad, read me every comment. All of them.

qa.q: What did the one criticism say about Jyoti's story?
qa.a: It said, 'The ending feels weak.'

qa.q: Why did Jyoti remember only the comment about the ending?
qa.a: The one criticism hurt, and hurt grabs attention, so the ten good notes faded and Jyoti came to see the whole story as weak.

qa.q: What turning point does Jyoti's story offer Rehana?
qa.a: Reading every comment aloud, slowly, showed how much had been skipped; Rehana can do the same with the essay before deciding it is bad.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel hearing that Masi nearly withdrew a story over one comment?
qa.a: Rehana may feel understood and a little lighter, seeing that even a grown-up once let one line outweigh ten, and may be willing to read every comment.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how, at fifteen, one criticism among ten praises was all she could remember, until the whole page was read aloud.

passage:
The power had been out since six, so Tanuja read her science project feedback by the light of her phone, which was at eight percent.

Zeenat Ma'am had written ten comments down the side of the water-filter report. "Excellent diagram." "Clear method." "Good use of local materials." "Neat tables." "Creative idea." Tanuja counted nine ticks like that. And at the bottom: "Your conclusion doesn't match your data. Please check."

The phone died.

In the dark, one line kept playing in her head: doesn't match your data. Doesn't match. She pictured Ma'am frowning as she wrote it. Ma'am must think I'm careless. The whole project is wrong.

The next morning, when her friend asked how the feedback was, Tanuja said, "Bad. Ma'am said my conclusion was wrong."

"Just that?"

Tanuja tried to remember the rest. She honestly couldn't. Something about a diagram, maybe.

qa.q: What did Zeenat Ma'am write at the bottom of the report?
qa.a: "Your conclusion doesn't match your data. Please check."

qa.q: Why can Tanuja remember only the criticism the next morning?
qa.a: The one line hurt, so her mind replayed it in the dark until it filled everything. The nine praises were dimmed because they didn't sting.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do to see the feedback more fairly?
qa.a: Reread the whole sheet in daylight and write the good comments and the one criticism side by side. Then she can fix the conclusion while remembering what she did well.

qa.q: If you were Zeenat Ma'am, how would you want Tanuja to read your comments?
qa.a: Ma'am would probably want Tanuja to feel proud of the nine good points and see the conclusion as one thing to fix. Ma'am likely didn't mean the project was wrong.

grounding: A teenage girl receives nine praises and one criticism on a project and can recall only the criticism, as the spotlight lands on what hurt.

passage:
After the school's annual day in Kolkata, Jeevan sir called Anirban to the music room. He had a feedback card for every soloist.

"Beautiful tone," he read aloud. "Great breath control. Good stage presence. You held the high note well. Your Bengali pronunciation was clear. Good eye contact. Confident entry. You listened to the tabla. You chose the right song." He paused. "The ending was a bit rushed. Slow it down next time."

Anirban said thank you and left.

That evening, when his mother asked how it went, he said, "Sir said I rushed the ending."

"What else?"

"Nothing much. Just that I rushed it." He went to his room and played the recording, skipping straight to the last thirty seconds, again and again. Each time, it sounded worse.

The card lay on his desk, face down.

qa.q: What did Jeevan sir say about the ending?
qa.a: "The ending was a bit rushed. Slow it down next time."

qa.q: Why does Anirban keep replaying only the last thirty seconds?
qa.a: The one criticism hurt, so his attention locks onto it and the nine praises fade. Replaying it makes the flaw feel bigger each time.

qa.q: What small step would help Anirban balance what he heard?
qa.a: Turn the card over and read every line aloud, maybe to his mother, then practise the ending slowly. That keeps the useful criticism without losing the praise.

qa.q: How might Jeevan sir feel if he heard Anirban say "Nothing much" about the feedback?
qa.a: Jeevan sir would probably be surprised and a little sad, having given nine real compliments. He meant the ending as a small tip, not the main message.

grounding: A teenager given nine praises and one criticism after a performance can only recall the criticism, as his mind's spotlight lands on what hurt.

passage:
Dear Jaya,
Guess what, I finally did my first solo at the temple festival on Saturday. And it was a disaster.
Well. Guru-ji said my footwork was sharp. And my costume was perfect, and my timing with the mridangam was the best in our batch, and my mudras were clean, and I remembered the whole varnam without a slip. Aunties came up after and said lovely things. But then Guru-ji said, 'Your abhinaya is still a little flat. Your face must tell the story.'
Flat. That's all I can think about. I lay in bed replaying it. Flat, flat, flat. I don't even remember what the aunties said properly now.
Write soon. Tell me about your exams.
Usha

qa.a: Jaya would probably notice the long list of praise and gently point out that the letter describes a success, not a disaster.

passage: Pradeep, you asked why I looked so miserable after the district debate. So here's the thing. The judges give you a feedback card, right? Mine had ten lines. passage:
Monday: Vinita ma'am returned Ayesha's science project with a page of comments. "Excellent research. Beautiful diagrams. Clear conclusion. Strong sources..." nine good lines. And at the bottom: "The hypothesis is unclear."

That evening her mother asked how it had gone. "Terrible. She said my hypothesis was unclear." That was all Ayesha could remember.

Wednesday: Ayesha still felt the sting. She told her friend, "Vinita ma'am thinks my project is bad." Her friend picked up the page and read it aloud, all nine good lines. Ayesha listened, surprised. She hadn't taken them in at all.

Saturday: Ayesha stuck the page on her wall, the nine good lines highlighted in yellow and the one about the hypothesis in pink. She rewrote the hypothesis in ten minutes. It had been one line.

qa.q: What did the last comment say?
qa.a: The last comment said, "The hypothesis is unclear."

qa.q: Why could Ayesha only remember the hypothesis comment?
qa.a: Ayesha felt hurt by the one criticism, and that sting drowned out the nine good comments.

qa.q: What did the highlighting on Saturday do?
qa.a: It made the nine good lines visible beside the one criticism, so Ayesha could fix the hypothesis without feeling the whole project was bad.

qa.q: How might Vinita ma'am feel if she knew Ayesha saw only the criticism?
qa.a: Vinita ma'am would likely be surprised and a bit sad, having written nine sincere praises.

passage:
Kamal, you're upset about one red line on your essay? Let your Gautam Dada tell you. At fifteen, in Varanasi, I wrote an essay on the river for a competition. The judge wrote a whole page: "Vivid images. Honest voice. Strong ending." Many good things. And one line: "Grammar careless in places."

Do you know what I remembered? Only "careless". For weeks I told everyone my essay was careless. I stopped writing for a whole year.

Then my teacher, Tripathi-ji, found the page in my bag and read it to me aloud, every line. He said, "You heard one sentence and made yourself deaf to nine." That was the turning point. I fixed my grammar, and I kept writing.

So, Kamal. Read me every line on your essay. Not just the red one.

qa.q: What was young Gautam's essay about?
qa.a: The essay was about the river.

qa.q: Why did young Gautam remember only "careless"?
qa.a: Young Gautam felt hurt and embarrassed by that one criticism, and it drowned out all the praise.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gautam keep writing?
qa.a: Tripathi-ji read every line of the page aloud, so Gautam heard the praise and fixed only the grammar.

qa.q: How might Tripathi-ji have felt finding the page in Gautam's bag?
qa.a: He was probably concerned that a talented student had stopped writing over one line, and wanted him to hear the rest.

grounding: A grandfather recalls hearing only one criticism among much praise for a boyhood essay, and giving up writing for a year.

passage:
The inter-school dance competition was held outdoors, in drizzle, and Parul danced with a heavy cold. Afterwards the judges handed each team a feedback card. Parul read it on the bus home.

"Excellent expressions. Great energy. Lovely costumes. Strong formations. Brave to perform in the rain. Good use of music." And at the bottom: "Parul's timing off in the second half."

By the time the bus reached her stop, she'd forgotten the rest. "They said I was off," she told her friend Tushar. "I ruined it for everyone."

Tushar held out his hand for the card. He read it slowly, all of it, then counted on his fingers. "Six good things, Parul. One about you. And you danced with a cold in the rain."

"But the timing..."

"Is one thing to practise. Not the whole card."

qa.q: What did the card say about Parul's timing?
qa.a: The card said, "Parul's timing off in the second half."

qa.q: Why did Parul feel she ruined it for everyone?
qa.a: Parul felt hurt and embarrassed by the one comment about her, and that single line pushed all the praise out of her mind.

qa.q: How did Tushar help Parul see the whole card?
qa.a: He read all of it and counted: six good things, one about Parul, and reminded her she had danced with a cold in the rain.

qa.q: How might Parul's teammates see the feedback card?
qa.a: They would likely focus on the praise and the brave performance, and might be surprised Parul saw only the timing comment.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who, after dancing in rain with a cold, can recall only the one criticism on a card full of praise.

"How was the art review?"
"Bad."
"Bad how, Farida?"
"Ma'am said the colours in my sky were muddy."
"What else did she say?"
"That's it. The sky was muddy."
Preeti picked up the feedback form from the table. "Farida, there's a whole paragraph here."
"I only saw the sky part."
"Listen. 'Strong composition. Lovely detail in the market scene. The faces are expressive. Good use of perspective. Shows real improvement since last term.' And then: 'Sky colours a little muddy; try fewer layers.'"
Farida was silent.
"That's five good things before the sky."
"I know. But the sky is all I can hear in my head."
"Why do you think that is?"
"Because I worked hardest on the sky."
"Okay. So fix the sky. But you're allowed to hear the other five too."

qa.q: What did Preeti do that helped?

qa.q: How might the art teacher feel if she knew Farida only remembered the sky?
qa.a: The teacher might be surprised and sorry, since she clearly wanted to praise real improvement.

passage:
Gargi ma'am returned our history essays on Friday. At the bottom of mine, she had written a whole note in green ink. I read it once in class and went home with one sentence in my head: "Your conclusion is weak." I thought about it at dinner. I thought about it in bed. By Sunday I was sure my essay was bad and I was bad at history.
On Monday my friend asked to see the note. She read it out loud: "Great argument. Well-chosen sources. Your paragraph on the salt march is the best in the class. Your writing has become much clearer. Your conclusion is weak; try ending with your strongest point."
I had read that whole note. I just hadn't kept any of it except the part that stung. Four good sentences, gone.
Now I read comments twice, and the second time I start from the top.
— Lalremsiami

qa.q: Which paragraph did Gargi ma'am call the best in the class?
qa.a: The paragraph on the salt march.

qa.q: Why did only "Your conclusion is weak" stay with Lalremsiami?
qa.a: That sentence stung and hurt, so it grabbed all the attention and made Lalremsiami forget the four good sentences.

qa.q: What habit did Lalremsiami build afterwards, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Reading comments twice, starting from the top the second time, so the praise gets noticed alongside the criticism.

qa.q: How might Gargi ma'am feel if she knew only one sentence was remembered?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and a bit sad, since she clearly wanted to encourage as well as correct.

grounding: A teenager looks back on remembering only the one critical line in a teacher's mostly glowing feedback, as hurt filtered out the rest.

passage:
Class 9 science fair, last week of Ramzan: note for my file.
Afreen's water-filter model drew a crowd all morning. I counted at least nine visitors who praised it. The judges liked the layered sand, two parents asked for the design, and the principal called it "properly thought through". One judge said the written report was too short.
At the end of the day Asif, her project partner, was grinning. Afreen was not. When I asked how it went, she said, "The report was bad. The judge said so." I asked what else people had said. She could remember only that one comment. She was fasting and tired, which did not help.
Next step: tomorrow I will go through the judges' sheets with her, every line, and let her mark the praise in green and the one fix in red.

qa.q: What did one judge say about Afreen's project?
qa.a: That the written report was too short.

qa.q: Why might the one criticism feel like the whole verdict to Afreen?
qa.a: The comment hurt, and hurt grabs attention; tired from fasting, Afreen feels disappointed and ashamed about the report, so the nine pieces of praise fade out.

qa.q: Is the teacher's plan a good countermeasure, and why?
qa.a: Yes. Going through every line and colouring the praise and the fix differently puts the whole picture back in view without pretending the criticism was never made.

qa.q: How might Asif see the same day?
qa.a: Asif, grinning, seems to remember the crowd and the praise, so Asif may be puzzled that Afreen looks so low after a day that felt like a success.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager who got plenty of praise and one criticism but can recall only the criticism.
